name: Tucker's Ice Cream
why: An 85-year-old Park Street parlor still making super-creamed ice cream from its founder's family recipes. Always owned by Alamedans, and still selling the Cho Cho.
story: Marshall and Verda Tucker were driving from Chico to open an ice cream shop in Santa Cruz in 1941, stopped in Alameda for lunch and stayed. Tucker's opened that June on Park Street using family recipes for super-creamed ice cream. It has changed hands several times, always to locals, and still runs flavor-naming contests.
order: A Cho Cho, the chocolate malt on a stick, or a Tommy Tucker: a vanilla cone dipped in chocolate.
practical: Ice cream cakes and fudge too
flags: Ownership as of 2018 (Zimmerman and Cook families); confirm current owners.
Original shop was at 1518 Park St; the current 1349 Park St spot came under a later owner, Kate Pryor.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Taqueria La Morena
why: A family taqueria serving downtown South San Francisco since 1986, known locally for big carne asada super burritos. Few written sources beyond its own site.
story: A family-owned taqueria on Baden Avenue in the old downtown of the Industrial City, open since 1986 and doing catering for the businesses east of the freeway. The menu is the classic taqueria run of tacos, quesadillas suizas and super burritos, and opens early on weekends.
hours: Mon to Fri 9:30 am to 8:30 pm; Sat and Sun 8 am to 8:30 pm (own site)
flags: Community/listing sources only.
Carne asada super burrito as the favorite comes from listing-site summaries.
Consider dropping unless a visit finds more to say.

name: Manley's Donut Shop
why: The Willow Glen donut shop that traces back to Clyde Manley's 1953 counter on Lincoln Avenue. Early-morning hours and a plain room.
story: Clyde Manley opened a donut shop at 1126 Lincoln Avenue around 1953. After he retired in 1977, the business moved a few doors up to 1080 Lincoln, where it still makes donuts from early morning. Several South Bay shops now carry the Manley name, but this is the one on the original block.
flags: Address changed: the candidate (1592 Meridian Ave) is a separate Manley Donuts opened around 2007. The 1953 history belongs to the Lincoln Ave shop, so the draft now points there; coordinates re-geocoded.
Who owns the Lincoln Ave shop now is not documented.
Community/listing sources only beyond the library history blog.

name: Minato
why: San Jose's oldest operating Japanese restaurant, still serving the brown curry rice it opened with. Owned by a couple who started there as staff in 1980.
story: Japantown's restaurants grew out of lunch counters for the farmworkers who arrived around 1900, and Minato keeps that home-style line going. It opened in 1961 and changed hands a few times before Gene and JoAnn Yoneda, who started there in 1980, bought it. The curry over rice and sukiyaki are original; the 1980s sushi bar is gone.
order: Curry over rice, or sukiyaki on a cold night.
practical: Lunch Tue to Sat 11:15 am to 1:15 pm
hours: Lunch Tue to Sat 11:15 am to 1:15 pm; dinner Tue to Thu 5 to 8 pm, Fri and Sat 5 to 8:30 pm (own site)
flags: Opening year conflicts: KQED says 1961, the restaurant's site says 1957. Story uses 1961.
Yonedas' start date (1980) comes from a search summary; KQED confirms they own it.
An Anthony Bourdain visit in 2015 appears in search summaries only; left out.

name: Dianda's Italian American Pastry
why: A Mission bakery in a building baking since 1906, run since 2003 by three of its own union bakers. Known for St. Honoré cakes and trays of Italian cookies.
story: Elio Dianda, a pastry chef from Lucca, bought a Mission Street bakery dating to 1906 and opened it under his name in 1962. His sons kept it going until 2003, when they sold to three longtime bakers, Sergio Flores, Luis Peña and Floyd Goldberg. Union bakers still start around 2 a.m. on the old recipes.
order: A slice of St. Honoré cake, or a mixed box of Italian cookies.
flags: Sale year: BCTGM and Mission Local point to 2003; an SF Heritage summary says 2004. Story uses 2003.
Ownership as of 2012; confirm the three co-owners are still there.
SF Heritage page did not render; Legacy Business status from its search summary.
Candidate listed evening; no evening hours found, dropped. Hours not confirmed.

name: Taqueria El Buen Sabor
why: A family-run Valencia Street taqueria open since 1995, still plain and cheap on a strip that has gentrified around it. Solid al pastor burrito, little else to say.
story: Open since 1995 on Valencia, a few blocks from Dolores Park, with a brightly painted front that has stayed while the street turned trendy around it. Still family-run, with everything made in house: slow-cooked meats, bright salsas and big burritos, long a standby for students and evening crowds.
hours: Daily 11 am to 9:30 pm (search summary of own site, confirm)
flags: Candidate listed it as late-night, but posted hours end at 9:30 pm; late dropped.
Tasting Table (Jan 2026) is a first-person local roundup.
Weak fit next to the Mission's better-known taquerias; consider dropping.

name: Brenda's French Soul Food
why: Chef Brenda Buenviaje's own brand of Southern and Creole cooking with French touches, best known for the crawfish beignet. Popular enough that weekend lines are the norm.
story: Chef Brenda Buenviaje opened this Polk Street room in 2007 to cook what she calls French soul food: Southern and Creole dishes with French technique. Banks, coworkers and even her parents declined to back her; a nonprofit lender came through. The crawfish-stuffed beignet became the signature, and she has since opened two more restaurants.
order: Crawfish beignet, then fried chicken or the fried bologna sandwich.
flags: Funding story (Opportunity Fund loan secured against her condo) comes from the Cameo page via search summary; not fetched.
One of three restaurants by the same chef (2022); not a chain, but more famous than most of this list. Fame may be closer to local-legend.
Weekend crowds may push it toward the hype-driven skip rule; Dan to judge.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Hai Ky Mi Gia
why: Little Saigon's main noodle house since 1987, cooking Teochew dishes rare in Cantonese-leaning San Francisco. The duck leg wonton noodle soup is the draw.
story: Since 1987 the anchor noodle house of Little Saigon, specializing in Teochew Chinese cooking that is rare in a Cantonese-leaning city. The big room has archways and hanging orchids. The duck leg is braised for hours with orange peel and herbs, then set over thick or thin egg noodles in wonton soup.
order: Wonton noodle soup with braised duck leg, thick egg noodles, and a strong iced coffee.
flags: Infatuation says it is busy at all times of day; morning opening not confirmed.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Eastern Bakery
why: Chinatown's oldest bakery, opened in 1924 as a bakery and diner, still mixing American pastries with Chinese ones. Its coffee crunch cake is a city classic.
story: Opened in 1924 as a bakery and diner, it is the oldest bakery in Chinatown, and the neon sign still reads Chinese and American food. The Kuan family bought it from the original owners in 1985. The cases still pair palmiers, lemon tarts and turnovers with pineapple buns and sesame balls; mooncakes use lotus paste made in house.
order: A slice of coffee crunch cake and a pineapple bun.
flags: Coffee crunch cake and in-house lotus paste come from the Spotlight Chinatown search summary; not fetched.
Bold Italic piece dates from 2017 (updated 2026); confirm the Kuan family still runs it.
Candidate listed evening; dropped. Hours not confirmed.

name: Sam Wo
why: A Chinatown jook house with roots around 1908, once famous for 3 a.m. closings, Beat poets and a notoriously rude waiter. Now on Clay Street, and revived in 2025 under new owners.
story: Sam Wo traces back to around 1908 on Washington Street, where it stayed open until 3 a.m., hosted Beat poets and employed Edsel Ford Fung, a waiter famous for insulting customers. It closed in 2012, reopened on Clay Street in 2015, then shut again when chef-owner David Ho retired in 2025. Two Bay Area restaurateurs reopened it that September.
practical: Reopened September 2025 with a mostly unchanged menu
New owners aim for later weekend hours
hours: Daily 11 am to 10 pm (Chronicle via search summary, Sept 2025)
flags: Founding date varies by source (1907, 1908, 1912); story says around 1908.
New owners Norris Song and Ming Duong (2025); the old room and staff are gone, so the atmosphere score is for the Clay St space.
Late hours were a plan in Sept 2025; late left off until confirmed.
Candidate fame local-legend kept.

name: Wing Lee Bakery
why: A cash-only Clement Street counter selling oversized dim sum, where a full meal costs under $10. The lunch line is mostly locals and nearby workers.
story: A small counter-service dim sum bakery on Clement, separate from Wing Lee BBQ next door. Metal trays and steamers hold barbecue pork buns the size of a saucer, extra-meaty siu mai and oversized fried sesame balls. Locals and nearby workers line up at lunch, and a full meal still comes in under $10.
order: Baked barbecue pork bun, pork siu mai and a sesame ball.
flags: Single editorial source (Infatuation, May 2023).
Late hours mentioned on aggregator sites only; left out.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Mandalay
why: San Francisco's oldest running Burmese restaurant, in a yellow room that looks permanently decorated for a party. Named a James Beard America's Classic in 2024.
story: Opened in February 1984 and now run by the married couple Kevin Chen and Sherry Dung, Mandalay is the oldest Burmese restaurant still operating in the city. The yellow dining room is hung with paper hearts, garlands and upside-down umbrellas, and staff stop to sing happy birthday several times a night. James Beard named it an America's Classic in 2024.
order: Tea leaf salad, then mohinga or a noodle soup with paratha.
flags: Fame raised from open-secret to local-legend: James Beard award (2024) and hours-long waits (Infatuation, Aug 2024).
Weekend waits may trip the hype rule; Dan to judge.
Candidate note called it quieter than the Clement Burmese spots; the Infatuation says otherwise, so that line was dropped.
SF Examiner article not fetched. Hours not confirmed.

name: Yuanbao Jiaozi
why: A tiny Irving Street room making boiled dumplings with thick, chewy wrappers in a glass-walled station by the door. Fourteen to an order, and there is often a line.
story: A small Irving Street shop with a few tables and a glass-walled station where staff fold dumplings in thick, chewy wrappers. The menu runs to a dozen boiled fillings, fourteen per order, from pork and napa cabbage to fish with shiitake. Bags of frozen dumplings sit in a freezer in the corner for later.
order: Pork and napa cabbage dumplings, plus the beef noodle soup if it is cold out.
flags: Opened 2018 (Hoodline headline, not fetched); owners not named in fetched sources.
Candidate note mentions a well-known clam dumpling; not in fetched sources, left out.
Area set to Central Sunset (Irving at 22nd Ave); candidate said Inner Sunset.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Deli Board
why: A takeout-only SoMa counter that stacks two or three meats per roll, with paper-thin pastrami as the anchor. Pricey at $18-23 a sandwich.
story: Adam Mesnick started Deli Board in 2009 and moved it to this Folsom Street counter two years later. The rule is more is more: corned beef, pastrami and salami on one roll, or bacon over tuna salad, dressed in house Board or Mick sauce, with a fat pickle on the side. Daily specials go further over the top.
order: The Allison, or anything built on the Romanian pastrami.
flags: Founding (2009) and move to 1058 Folsom (2011) come from a search summary; Hoodline 2015 profile not fetched.
Owner runs a polarizing SoMa street-conditions social account (Chronicle, 2023); possible brand fit issue for Dan.
Price point is high for this list.
Confirm still open in 2026: newest fetched source is Feb 2024.
Hours not confirmed.
